Fiji has since 2019 developed numerous policies aimed at mitigating the adverse effects of climate change, such as the National Disaster Risk Reduction Policy of 2018 to 2039 and the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction. These policies, Mr. Vice President, expand the mandate for the disaster legislation to not only cover natural hazards, but also other potential hazards that may cause disasters, including biological, environmental, geological or geophysical, hydro-meteorological and technological hazards, with the exception of civil unrest and terrorism. Fiji's dedication to climate resilience and environmental justice is further highlighted in innovative initiatives. such as the nature-based sea walls, the National Adaptation Registry, and community-based disaster risk management programs. While our climate resilient initiatives reflect a forward-thinking approach to safeguarding vulnerable communities, our constitutional framework champions equality and prohibits discrimination, on multiple grounds. Together, these efforts form the foundation of a more equitable and sustainable future for all Fijians. Fiji has also constitutional provisions that address discrimination on the basis of disability, race, age, gender, sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, religion, amongst other prohibited grounds of discrimination. Mr. Vice President, Fiji has also taken steps to address discrimination at the structural level, whether it is discrimination in education, in accessing institutions for justice, or indeed in access to other services. For instance, the Fiji Human Rights and Anti-Discrimination Commission has an expanded anti-discrimination mandate under the constitution to receive, to investigate, and to take steps to secure appropriate redress if human rights have been violated, including making applications to the courts for redress or for other forms of relief or remedies. In terms of education, Fiji continues to uphold its commitment to providing equitable opportunities for all its citizens. The tertiary scholarship and loan service, which has been in operation since its inception in 2015, exemplifies this commitment. This initiative ensures that scholarships are awarded solely based on merit, irrespective of race, gender, religion, gender identity and expression. This fund is designed to provide financial support to Fijian students who have qualified for higher education at appropriate tertiary institutions but are unable to support themselves financially. By doing so, the tertiary scholarship and loan service increases equitable access to higher education, enabling students from diverse backgrounds to pursue their academic goals at affordable rates. Mr. Vice President, Fiji remains committed to dismantling systemic and structural discrimination. which will allow every Fijian to realize their full potential and to celebrate their inherent dignity as humans. The open merit recruitment and selection process within the Fijian civil service has enabled all Fijians, regardless of color, creed, gender, or any other prohibited ground of discrimination, and equal opportunity to gainful employment. We recognize that the root cause of such violence stems from patriarchal attitudes towards women and girls. To address this, Fiji launched the National Action Plan to Prevent Violence Against All Women and Girls, 2023 to 2028. This was a historic milestone for Fiji, becoming the first ever Pacific Island country alongside Australia to develop an inclusive, evidence-based plan aimed at eliminating gender-based violence and to empower women and girls. Mr. Vice President, This inclusive, whole-of-government initiative focuses on prevention through education, awareness campaigns, and systemic reforms. It emphasizes collaboration with civil society, community leaders, and international partners to create an environment where women and girls are able to live free from fear, and harm. Our Fiji police force operates a no drop policy ensuring all cases of gender-based violence are handled with zero tolerance and no reconciliation. Health services are also equipped with national gender-based violence guidelines enabling healthcare professionals to provide appropriate care and support to survivors. Fiji has also made progress in empowering women economically, recognizing that financial independence is critical to breaking cycles of violence and poverty. Programs like the National Women's Expo and the Fiji Women's Economic Empowerment National Action Plan of 2024-2029 provide platforms and resources for women to thrive as entrepreneurs and leaders. Mr. Vice President, as Fiji takes significant steps to address gender-based violence, It also recognizes the importance of freedom of expression, assembly, and association in fostering a healthy and democratic society. In April 2023, the repeal of the Media Industry Development Act, the acronym for which is MIDAR, was a landmark step in restoring media freedom. allowing journalists to report independently without fear of prosecution. This action significantly improved Fiji's ranking in the World Press Freedom Index from 89 to 44. Fiji has also reformed its approach to public gatherings under the Public Order Act of 2014. While permits are still required, the process has become more transparent and inclusive, ensuring that refusals are based on justified grounds. For example, in 2023 alone, 1,126 permits were approved, reflecting Fiji's commitment to facilitating peaceful assemblies. A key demonstration of these freedoms was a public march on the 25th of August 2023, when women's rights organizations peacefully protested the planned disposal of Fukushima wastewater into the Pacific Ocean. This event, like many others, highlighted Fiji's respect for the right to peaceful assembly and its support for civic participation. While guaranteeing these freedoms, Fiji remains vigilant against incitement to violence, hate speech, and discrimination, aligning with the limitations provided under our constitution and international conventions and norms. Building on this framework of human rights and protections, Fiji has also made notable progress in addressing serious crimes like human trafficking, modern day slavery, and child labor. In 2017, Fiji exceeded to the United Nations Convention against Transnational Organized Crime and the Protocol to Prevent, Suppress and Punish Trafficking in Persons, especially women and children. This marked a pivotal step in aligning Fiji's national efforts with international standards, reaffirming our commitment to protecting vulnerable populations, especially women and children. At the heart of our legal framework is section 10 of the Fiji Constitution, which guarantees freedom for all Fijians from slavery, servitude, forced labour and human trafficking. Complementing this is the 2009 Crimes Act, which encompasses and includes provisions to address human trafficking, both trafficking in persons as well as trafficking in children. These robust legislative measures underscores Fiji's zero tolerance stance towards these crimes. Mr. Vice President, recognizing the need for a coordinated and victim centered approach, Fiji's Ministry of Home Affairs and Immigration, in collaboration with key stakeholders, has developed a national referral mechanism and standard operating procedures. This mechanism provides a structured framework to ensure that victims of trafficking are supported from their initial identification to prosecution and eventual reintegration into society. In 2021, Fiji took a significant step forward with the launch of its National Anti-Human Trafficking Strategy and its accompanying National Action Plan. These initiatives lay out a comprehensive roadmap of activities to combat trafficking, focusing on prevention, protection, as well as prosecution. Mr. Vice President, building capacity within our institutions and raising awareness are key pillars of our national efforts. While these legal frameworks provide essential protections, Mr. Vice President, in addressing serious crimes, Fiji has faced unprecedented challenges in recent years, particularly those in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic. The COVID-19 pandemic presented quite significant challenges for Fiji, but it also underscored our resilience and commitment to protecting human rights under quite extraordinary circumstances. Human and financial resource constraints combined with the escalating impacts of climate change do present and will continue to present significant challenges. To address first some of the recommendations, particularly on torture and the use of force. Since Fiji's ratification of UNCAC in 2016, we have embarked on a first hour procedure project which ensures the provision of legal counsel to every suspect at the police station within one hour of arrest with a protocol guiding the conduct of both police and lawyers in relation to the implementation of that right. There have been reforms of policies and procedures within our police force and particularly the recording of interviews of arrested or detained persons, in addition to the counsel that they have already provided in order to decrease incidents of police brutality during investigations and interrogation of persons. On the themes that have emerged from the various recommendations relating to human rights defenders, and civil society organizations. Fiji's robust bill of rights provisions provide that every person has the right to freedom of speech, expression, thought, opinion, and publication, which includes the freedom to seek, receive, and impart information, the freedom of the press in all forms, and the freedom of imagination and creativity, as well as the academic freedom and scientific research. Fiji indeed recognizes the independence and contribution of human rights defenders. And such organizations are part of national task forces and committees that are chaired at government level and indeed to take on board their voices. There is recognition that because this is These rights of human rights defenders are protected under the Fijian constitution. And the civil societies and minority groups participation in national public debates indeed taken on board as necessary and a crucial element to deliberative democracy. Of course, our parliament, through its standing committees, play a vital role by actively engaging through the consultation process on various matters with members of the public, including civil societies. Turning to the recommendations that have been made with respect to climate change, disaster risk management, and the environment, Indeed, as has been mentioned earlier by the Honorable Attorney General, Fiji has a standalone Ministry of Environment and Climate Change with a minister who's been sworn in to oversee and lead that ministry. And national coordination is taken through the National Climate Change Coordination Committee that deals with planning, mitigation, and adaptation efforts. There are legislations that are in place, in particular the Climate Change Act that was promulgated in 2021 and the National Disaster Risk Management Act, which facilitates the work that the government does through the ministry that was implemented last year. And this takes on board the prioritized focus on gender equality, disability and social inclusion in climate actions and planned relocations. the national disaster awareness week is an initiative that allows for members of the public to be engaged and be involved in the promotion of resilience, including the launching of a family safety plan mobile app for households to help them in disaster readiness. The provision of monetary support for back to school assistance, as well as transport assistance to those from low income households.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President. In relation to the recommendations on gender-based violence and implementation of the Fiji National Action Plan to prevent violence against all women and girls, Fiji wishes to state that further to this, Fiji is also actively involved in the various initiatives and campaigns to address gender-based violence. For example, under the Fiji's Ministry of Health, a national gender-based violence guidelines for health was launched in 2023 and conducted regional training for trainers followed by a national training of trainers in Fiji. It also facilitated a nationwide rollout of gender-based violence guidelines in the same year, offers expert medical care, treatment and referrals of to gender-based violence victims. It provides clinical management, include forensic investigations in a private and confidential setting, ensures the presence of health staff of the opposite sex for clients below 18 years of age, allows clients above 18 years to provide consent for the presence of additional health staff. And requires the presence of a neutral adult female person welfare officer and female police officer when a medical officer or nurse practitioner or nurse is alone. It collects forensic materials and delivers them to investigation police officers and records all investigations and outcomes to patients folders and registers. Further to these initiatives under Fiji's Ministry of Health, by the Ministry of Health, the Fiji Police Force also runs the Nduavatu Community Policing Awareness Initiative Program whereby they organize community symposium, radio talks and crime stoppers to raise awareness on gender-based violence. or they also implement initiatives like neighborhood watch zone, the blue light program and policing through sports to advocate against gender-based violence and sexual offenses and conducts gender-based violence trainings and awareness programs with government and non-government organization. The Fiji Police Force also has a no-drop policy as the Attorney General had mentioned earlier for a stringent compliant institutional stance of zero tolerance and no reconciliation for any case of gender-based violence, domestic violence and sexual offences complaints. These are some of the initiatives further to the launch of the Fiji National Action Plan to prevent violence against all women and girls.
